Proletariat

proh-luh-TAIR-ee-ut · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Proletariat is the working class; the group of wage-earning workers, especially those without significant property or capital.

The economist argued that the modern proletariat looks very different from the factory workers of the 1800s, but still shares the same basic position in the economy.

Worked Example

The novel's opening chapter describes the exhausted proletariat pouring out of the textile mills at dawn, their wages barely enough to cover rent.

Proletariat refers to the working class as a whole group, not to any one individual worker -- it's typically used when discussing economics, history, or politics.

How Proletariat Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

workforce

workforce: the group of people who work in a particular industry or country

working class

working class: the social class of people who work for wages, especially in manual or industrial jobs

Antonyms

aristocracy

aristocracy: a ruling class of people with hereditary titles and privilege

elite

elite: a select group considered to be the best or most privileged

How Strong Is It? — workforce → proletariat → masses

workforce vs. proletariat

workforce vs. proletariat: Workforce is a neutral, everyday term for everyone who works, without proletariat's specific class and history-loaded meaning.

masses vs. proletariat

masses vs. proletariat: The masses pushes the idea even further, referring broadly to the general population, especially as distinct from any ruling or elite group.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

root — proles

root — proles: offspring, progeny (Latin proles, 'offspring')

suffix — -ariat

suffix — -ariat: a group or class of people (Latin -arius)

Put it together

Put it together: Proletariat comes from Latin proles ('offspring'), since ancient Roman law counted the poorest citizens as contributing to the state only through having children -- a proletarius owned nothing else of value except future generations.

Use the root in a new word: prolific

Use the root in a new word: prolific: A prolific author -- one who produces many books -- shares proletariat's Latin root proles, since prolific literally means 'producing offspring or output.'
